activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
story:
Anthony went to the library with his mom. Ms. Bui smiled at the big desk. "Would you like your own card?" she asked. Anthony nodded. The card was orange and shiny. It had his name on it. He held it with both hands.

Anthony found a book about dinosaurs. It smelled like paper and old glue. He hugged it tight. "I want to keep it forever," he said. Ms. Bui shook her head gently. "It has to come back by a certain day," she said. "That day is called the due date." She stamped a little paper. One book, one card, one due date.

Anthony read the book at home, one page, two pages, three pages. Then he met his friend Alaia at the library. She wanted to read the dinosaur book too. Anthony gave it to Ms. Bui at the desk. "Here you go," he said. Alaia took it next. "My turn," she said. Anthony picked a new book about trucks. His mom took his hand, and they walked home together.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Lydia was at home. Her friend Laith came to play. Laith had big tears on his face. He was crying.

"Why are you crying?" Lydia asked.

"I lost my dog toy," Laith said. "He was my best toy. Now I feel so sad."

Lydia felt sad too. She did not want Laith to cry. She ran to her room. She looked under her bed. She looked in her toy box.

Then Lydia found her favorite dog. It was brown and soft. She held it tight. It was hard to give it away. But Laith was still crying.

"Here," Lydia said. "You can hold my dog."

Laith wiped his eyes. He hugged the soft dog. His tears stopped. Then he smiled a big smile.

"Thank you," Laith said. "I feel happy now."

Lydia smiled too. She saw one thing. When Laith felt sad, he cried. When he felt better, the crying stopped.

"Can my dog spell too?" Laith asked. "I can spell my name. L, A, I, T, H."

Lydia laughed. "Dogs cannot spell. But my dog can sit!"

Lydia made the dog sit on the rug. Laith clapped his hands. He was excited.

They played until it got late. Then Laith's dad came to the door.

"Time to go home," his dad said.

"Can I keep the dog?" Laith asked.

"You can borrow him," Lydia said. "Bring him back soon."

Laith waved from the car. Lydia waved back from her window. Her mom gave her a warm hug.

"You were kind today," Mom said.

Lydia held her mom's hand. "Laith can bring my dog tomorrow," she said.

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
story:
Arya went to the library with her family. She wanted the big red book about trucks. But Nolan had it first. "Can I have it?" asked Arya. "After me," said Nolan. "One turn for you, one turn for me."

Arya watched Nolan turn the pages. One page, two pages, three pages. Then Nolan held out the book. "Your turn," he said. Arya smiled and took it.

Nearby, a family sat by the window. The mama was rocking a baby. The baby was sleeping. Arya got excited and shouted, "Trucks!" The baby woke up and began to cry. The mama rocked and rocked. Arya felt bad. The crying sounded scary.

Ms. Nikolaidis came over. She bent down close. "The baby is sleeping," she whispered. Arya looked at the baby. She looked at Ms. Nikolaidis. Then she made her voice very small. "One truck," she whispered. "Two trucks. Three trucks."

The baby's eyes closed. The crying stopped. The mama rocked some more. Soon the baby was sleeping again. Arya turned one page, then another, all in her quiet voice. Nolan came back and sat close. "Trucks," he whispered. Arya nodded and slid the book so they could both see.

The baby slept and slept. The library was quiet and warm.

story:
Milan sat on his bed with his big dog book. He loved the dog with one brown eye. "Who drew this dog?" he asked.

He took the book to his mom. "Can you help me look?" She opened the front cover. She turned to the first page. There was a name there. "Here it is," she said. "The person who draws the pictures for a book is called the illustrator."

"An illustrator," said Milan. "She drew my dog!" He ran back to his room. He held the book up high.

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
story:
The lights went out. It was dark in the backyard. Juliette could not see her toys. She wanted her teddy bear on the chair.

Juliette ran to the chair. Bump! Her leg hit the chair. "Ow," she said. It was too dark to run.

Dad came out with a big flashlight. He turned it on. Juliette could see the chair. She could see her teddy, too. "My leg bumped the chair," Juliette said. "It was not a mean chair. The dark made me bump it."

"In the dark, walk slowly," said Dad. He held out his hand. "Hold my hand so nobody trips." Juliette held Dad's hand. They walked slowly, step by step, back across the grass. Nothing bumped them at all.

They sat on the step together. Juliette found a feather on the ground. It was soft and white. She let it go and watched it float down. Dad shone the flashlight on it. The feather danced in the light. Juliette laughed and let it float again.

Soon the lights came back on. The house glowed. "Now we can see everything," said Juliette. She held Dad's hand all the way to the door and carried her teddy inside.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Everett woke up in his bed. The sun was bright in his window. He heard a clink and a pour. Was someone in the kitchen? He wanted pancakes today.

He padded down the hall. Mom and Dad sat at the table. There were plates and cups and a big pancake stack. "Good morning," said Everett.

"Good morning," said Mom. "It is morning now. Morning is when we wake up and eat breakfast." She put a warm pancake on his plate. Everett took a big bite. Yum.

Yesterday there were no pancakes. Yesterday they had eggs. "Pancakes today," said Everett. "Eggs yesterday." Dad laughed. "That's right. And tomorrow we can have pancakes again, if you want."

"Tomorrow is after I sleep again?" asked Everett. Dad nodded. "Yes. First today, then sleep, then tomorrow." Everett thought that was a funny order. But he liked it.

After breakfast, Everett wanted to play a game. "Can we play now?" he asked. "We can play later," said Dad. "First the dishes go in the sink." Everett helped carry his cup. He was careful and slow.

Then it was time for the game. Everett and Dad sat on the rug. "I go first," said Everett. He rolled the dice. He moved his little piece two spaces. "Your turn, Dad," he said. Dad smiled and rolled the dice too.

Everett yawned a big yawn. Morning was for pancakes. Later was for games. Sleep would come after that. He leaned on Dad's arm and whispered, "Good morning was good." Dad said, "Good morning still is." Everett rolled the dice one more time.

activity: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
story:
Eleanor sat at the paint table at summer camp. She wanted to paint green grass. But there was no green paint. All the pots were empty except yellow and blue. How would her grass look right?

Rudy sat next to her. He was painting a blue lake. "No green," said Eleanor. "My grass needs green." She looked and looked at the pots.

Then she had an idea. What if the paints could be friends? She dipped her brush in the yellow pot. She dabbed yellow on the paper. Then she dipped the same brush in the blue pot. She swirled the wet blue into the wet yellow spot.

The spot turned green! Real green, like real grass. "Look, look!" said Eleanor. Rudy leaned over. "Green!" he said. "How did you do that?" Eleanor made a big green field. She even gave her painting a green coat of grass at the bottom.

Mr. Wu came to see. "That is lovely grass," he said. Eleanor held up her wet brush. "Yellow and blue made it," she said. "Yellow plus blue." Then she dipped her brush again. "Can blue and yellow make more?" she asked. Mr. Wu smiled and slid two full pots down the table toward her.

activity: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
story:
Today was Eliana's birthday. Her mom brought cupcakes to school. Ms. Goldberg said, "We will sing for you." Eliana felt worried. She did not like loud singing. She asked her mom, "Will it be very loud?" Her mom said, "Not too loud. Just wait and listen."

Robyn and Clementine helped set out the napkins. Eliana helped too. She carried one cupcake very slowly. Then she had to sneeze. The cupcake began to drop. Clementine caught it with a plate. "Safe!" said Clementine. The cupcake was fine.

Then everyone stood up. They sang, "Happy birthday to you." Eliana waited. Then she heard it. They sang, "Happy birthday, dear Eliana." They were singing her name. She hid her big smile behind her hands. Her cheeks felt warm and happy.

After the song, Ms. Goldberg gave out the cupcakes. Eliana looked at hers. There was a tiny toy duck sitting on top. "A duck!" said Eliana. "For me?" "Yes," said Ms. Goldberg. "It is yours to keep." Eliana put the duck in her pocket. She held up her cupcake and said, "Sing again, please. I want to hear my name one more time."

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Madelyn found a book on her bed. It was a book about a puppy who could chase butterflies.

She opened the book from the back. "That is funny," she said. The puppy was already home. The butterflies were gone. The story was all mixed up!

"What a mixed-up day," said Madelyn. She turned a page. Now the puppy was wet. Then he was dry. Then he was sleepy. "What a mixed-up day," she said again.

Grandpa peeked in the door. "That story sounds funny," he said. He sat down on the bed with her. Madelyn showed him the pages. Grandpa turned the book around in his hands.

Madelyn looked at the front. She saw the puppy at the start. He was a small puppy, waking up. She turned the pages one by one. The puppy chased a blue butterfly. He ran past a nice red flower. He splashed in a puddle. At the end, the puppy went home to sleep.

"So that is his day," said Madelyn. She patted the back cover. "Good night, puppy." Then she hugged the book tight.

"Shall we mix up the cards and play one more time?"

activity: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
story:
Elliot ran to the bathroom at summer camp. He used the toilet. Then he ran out fast. The water slide was calling him. "Wait for me, Theia!" he shouted.

Theia was at the sink. She was rubbing soap on her hands. "We always wash our hands after using the toilet," she said. She made soap bubbles shaped like a cloud. Elliot giggled and ran back.

Ms. Chowdhury was by the sinks. She helped Elliot pump the soap. "Now we count to twenty," she said. They sang the camp song twice. Elliot scrubbed and scrubbed. The soap smelled like lemons. He sniffed his hands. His nose was happy. "Not yucky anymore!" he said.

Mavrick zoomed out of the bathroom without washing. "Come back, Mavrick!" Elliot called. Mavrick ran back to the sink. He washed his hands too. All three friends sang the song together.

Then they ran to the water slide. Splash! The water was cold. Elliot's hands were clean and wet. Theia held up her soapy-smelling hands. "Twenty seconds, best seconds," she said. Elliot laughed. "Wash first, splash after!" he said. And he brought his clean hands all the way to the top.

story:
Asher stood by the grocery store door. His coat was on, but the zipper was stuck at the bottom. He pulled it up, up, up. It went a little way and stopped. He pulled again. This time it slid all the way to his chin. "I did it," he said. His mom clapped.

One red mitten fell off the shelf by the door. Asher picked it up. Where was the other one? He looked under the cart. He looked by the bread. "Mom, where do mittens go?" he asked. She smiled and pointed at his coat. "Look at your side," she said. Asher patted his hip. There was a little door there. He opened it. Inside was the other red mitten!

Asher tucked both mittens into the pocket. He pushed the little door shut. They fit just right. He patted the pocket. It felt squishy and soft, like two small pillows.

The cart rolled past the soap aisle. Asher smelled flowers and lemons. Then a spot of dust slid under his shoe. He swept it away with his toe. At the checkout, Asher pulled both mittens out of the pocket. "Look, Ms. Cashier," he said. "My pocket kept them safe!" He put them back in, one, two, and zipped his coat up all by himself again.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Luke went to the park early with his dad. The sun made everything warm. Luke touched the slide. The slide felt hot. He pulled his hand back fast. "That part is in the sun," his dad said. They waited under a tree. Luke watched the shade creep over the slide. He touched it again. Now it was cool.

Zoya and Daxon came to the park too. They all ran to the sandbox. Luke stayed where his dad could see him. He found a picnic table under a big tree. On the table sat a small bag. Little round things spilled out of it. They were red and yellow and green. They looked like candy.

Luke wanted to pick one up. They were so pretty, like a tiny rainbow. But he stopped his hand. He remembered what his mom had told him. Only a grown-up gives you medicine, even if it looks like candy.

"I will go get a grown-up," Luke said. He did not touch the little round things. He walked back to his dad. His dad held his hand. They went to the table together. His dad looked at the bag. "These are pills," his dad said. "You did the right thing."

A woman came running back. She had been looking for her bag. She thanked Luke. "I did not touch them," Luke said. She smiled at him. Zoya and Daxon clapped. Then they all went back to the sandbox. Luke dug a deep hole. It felt cool and soft under his hands.

story:

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
story:
Zachary looked out the window. Snow was falling on the backyard. "No school today," said his dad. "It is a snow day."

Zachary put on his boots. He put on his red mittens. He went outside to play. The snow was soft and cold. It squeaked under his boots. He patted a big snowball. It was round like a ball.

"I want to keep this snowball," Zachary said. His dad helped him carry it inside. They put it in a bowl on the table. Zachary wanted to save it for tomorrow.

Zachary played with his toy butterfly. He painted a picture of the snow. He waited a long time. Then he looked at the bowl. The snowball was small now. The bowl was not empty. There was water in it. "Dad, come look!" said Zachary. "The snow turned into water."

"The snow melted in here," said his dad. "It is warm inside." Zachary touched the water. It was cool on his finger.

Zachary had an idea. He got a fresh snowball from the yard. He put it in a cup. He carried the cup outside to the cold porch. "Stay there, snowball," he said.

The next morning, Zachary checked his cup. The snowball was still there, big and white. Zachary smiled and patted it with his mitten.

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
Grandma was coming to stay for a week. Ali wanted to make her feel happy. He got out a big bowl. Mom said, "I will pour the milk. You can pass me the spoon." Ali passed the spoon. Mom stirred pancake batter. The stove was hot, so Mom stood near it. Ali stood back and watched.

Then Ali saw a photo on the fridge. It showed Grandma holding Mom's hand. Mom was little in the photo. Ali frowned. "That is the wrong photo," he said. "Grandma is not your mom." Mom laughed softly. "Yes, she is. Grandma is my mom." Ali looked at the photo again. So Grandma was a mom two times!

The doorbell rang. Grandma came in with her bag. Ali ran to hug her legs. "You are Mom's mom!" he said. Grandma smiled a big smile. "That is my best hug today," she said. Then they all ate warm pancakes together.

activity: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
story:
Alexander stood in the big school gym. Mr. Dang put a hoop on the floor. He put three beanbags in a red basket. "Try to throw one in," said Mr. Dang. Alexander threw the first beanbag. It landed far from the hoop. He threw the second one. It bounced off the edge. Would the third one go in? He threw it. It went in! Alexander clapped his hands. He liked the sound of the beanbag landing inside.

Then Mr. Dang brought out a big yellow ball. He rolled it to Axton. Axton caught it. He rolled it to Harley. Harley caught it. Then it was Alexander's turn. The ball came rolling fast. Alexander's hands were tucked in his pockets. The ball bumped his legs and rolled away.

"Try again," said Mr. Dang. He rolled the ball again. This time Alexander held his arms out. His hands were open and wide. The big ball came right into them. He caught it! "I caught it!" said Alexander. He looked at his open hands. Arms out, hands open. That is what got him ready.

They played a counting game around the circle. One roll for Axton. One roll for Harley. One roll for Alexander. Around and around the ball went. Then the ball rolled past everyone. It rolled under the snowy coats hanging on the wall. It stopped on a sneaker. Whose sneaker was that? Out stepped the coach. "Looking for this?" he said, holding up the big yellow ball.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
story:
Amira was on a big train with her dad. They were going to Grandma's house. It was far, far away from home.

Amira looked out the window. She saw white clouds. She saw a river with water in it. "Can I have a drink?" she asked. Her dad gave her a water bottle. One sip, two sips, three sips.

Then Dad looked worried. "Oh no," he said. "Which stop is ours? I forgot." A lady in a blue coat came by. Her name was Ms. Desir. She pointed to a big paper on the train wall. "Look here," she said. "This is a map."

Amira stood up and looked. The map showed little dots for places. It showed the road the train went on. Amira put her finger on the map. She found the river on the map. She found the river out the window. "There!" she said. "The river is here, so we are here." Then she moved her finger along. One dot, two dots, three dots. "This dot is Grandma's town."

Dad smiled. "The map shows us the way," he said. The train went on. Soon a voice said, "Next stop, Grandma's town." Amira held her dad's hand. The train slowed down and stopped.

There was Grandma, waving on the platform.

"I want to spread the butter," said Jasper. Mama gave him a small knife with a rounded end. Jasper dipped it in the butter. He spread it across the toast. It went bump, bump, bump. Little lumps sat on top. He spread them flat. The toast was all shiny now.

Next came the milk. Jasper held the cup. He poured and poured. The milk came up to the very top. He walked to the table. Oh no! The milk tipped over the edge. It made a puddle on the floor.

Mama wiped the puddle. "Try again," she said. Jasper poured once more. This time he stopped before the cup was full to the top. He walked slowly to the table. Not one drop fell out. He sat down and took a big bite of buttery toast and a big sip of milk.

Then something small and funny happened. The cat trotted in and licked the last bit of spilled milk right off the floor.

"That was Onyx's treat," Jasper said with a laugh. Onyx bumped his leg and purred.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Jaxson looked out the window. The sky was white. Snow was falling on the backyard.

"Snowy day," said Mom. "Put on your boots."

Jaxson pulled on his boots. He zipped his big coat. He ran outside into the snow. His friend Jaiden was already there. Jaiden wore a hat, a scarf and red mittens.

"Let's make a snow wall," said Jaiden.

They patted the snow. They stacked it up. Soon they had a big white wall. It was tall as their knees.

Then Jaxson tried to roll a snowball. The snow felt cold. His hands turned red. They hurt. He dropped the snowball and held his hands.

"My hands are cold," he said.

Jaiden held out his red mittens. "Mittens keep my hands warm," he said. "Try yours."

Jaxson looked down. His mittens were in his coat pocket. He pulled them on. He rolled a new snowball. His hands felt warm. He patted it onto the wall.

From the door, Ms. Suzuki, the neighbour, called, "Cocoa is ready!"

The boys went in slowly. Their legs were sleepy from playing. Mom set two warm cups on the table.

Jaxson took a sip. Something was floating in his cocoa. It was a tiny marshmallow snowman, with little stick arms.

"He looks just like us," said Jaxson, and he waved at it.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
story:
Jaxon sat on his bedroom floor. He had a new wallet. Inside was his new card. It had his name on it. "Jaxon," he read out loud. He felt shy about it. He hid it under his pillow.

At the library, Jaxon found a big red book. It had a bear on the front. He hugged it tight. "Can I keep it?" he asked his mom.

"Ask the lady at the desk," she said.

Jaxon felt shy. He walked slowly. He slid his card across the desk. "What is this for?" he asked.

The lady smiled. "It is a library card. It lets you borrow books and take them home."

Jaxon's eyes got big. "Take it home? To my room?"

"Yes," she said. "You can bring it back soon."

Jaxon gave her his card. She zipped it through a machine. Beep! She put the red book in his hands.

"You mean it is mine now?" he asked.

"It is yours for a while," she said.

Jaxon held the book all the way home. He ran to his bedroom. He sat on his bed. He opened the red book. The bear smiled at him. Jaxon smiled too.

"Mom," he called. "My card made this happen. Can we go back tomorrow?"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Brielle went to the park with her red ball. She wanted to kick it to Reginald. She kicked it high. The ball went into the cozy little playhouse at the park.

The playhouse was dark inside. Brielle stepped in to find her ball. She looked and looked. "It is hard to tell what color things are in here," she said. Everything looked the same dark gray. She touched something round. Was this her ball? She could not tell.

She carried it out into the sun. In the bright light, she could see. The ball in her hands was green, not red. It was Reginald's green ball! Then Reginald called from the doorway. He held up a red ball. "Is this yours?" he asked. "Yes!" said Brielle. They traded balls and laughed. Then they kicked the balls by the duck pond. The red ball went far. The green ball went far, too. Brielle read her name on the red ball. It was her ball, for sure.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
story:
Leo went to the farm with his class. Ms. Foster said, "Today we will name our five senses." Leo wanted to try them all before snack time.

First Leo used his eyes. He saw a cow with a short tail. Then he used his nose. He sniffed hay, and it smelled sweet. He touched a soft leaf on a plant. He used his tongue to taste his apple at snack time.

Then a big truck rumbled by. The noise was loud. Leo put his hands over his ears. The sound got quieter, just like that. He took his hands off. The truck was loud again. He put his hands back on. Quiet again!

"Ms. Foster, my ears can hear," said Leo. "And my hands make it quiet." Asha laughed and covered her ears too. The cows went back to munching their hay.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
Joshua was in the backyard with Grandma. Grandma was staying for a whole week. Joshua had a red ball. "Grandma, play with me!" he said. Grandma threw the ball, but it went weak and slow. "I am tired," she said. "I need to rest." Joshua found her a chair in the shade.

Joshua still wanted to play. "I wish someone could play ball," he said. Grandma smiled. "I know a story instead," she said. "It is about your dad." Joshua sat down. "Dad is big," he said. "Dad was little once," said Grandma. "He had a small blue bike. He fell off. He cried. Then he got on again."

Joshua laughed. "Dad on a little bike!" he said. "Tell more!" Grandma told about Dad and his sister, who hid Dad's shoe. Joshua asked, "Can you tell stories every day this week?" "Every day," said Grandma. Joshua ran to get her a blanket for her lap. "Story time!" he called. "Story time!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
story:
The cultural center was full of people. Theo held his dad's hand. The night was coming, and lanterns glowed up high. "Stay close," said his dad. "It is a big crowd."

Theo saw a food stall. It smelled sweet. He let go of his dad's hand. He took one step. Then two steps. The people were tall and thin between him and the stall. He could not see his dad. Theo's tummy felt small.

He stopped walking. He looked back. There was his dad! Theo ran to him and grabbed his hand. He held on tight. "I stayed close," said Theo. His dad smiled. They walked to the food stall together, hand in hand. "One sweet bun, please," said his dad.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Juliette went to the park with her mama. Jimmy was there too. He had a big cardboard box.

"I want to sit in it," said Jimmy. He sat down inside.

Juliette wanted a turn. She waited. Then Jimmy got out.

Juliette sat in the box. She held the sides. "Beep beep!" she said. "This box is my car!"

Jimmy looked sad. "I want it to be a car too."

"Okay," said Juliette. "You can ride in my car."

Then Jimmy had an idea. "Let's make it a boat," he said. He turned the box and rocked it side to side. "Row, row!"

"The box can be a house too," said Juliette. She tipped it up on one side. It made a little wall. Jimmy laughed and crawled in behind her.

Rosie came over with her toy elephant. "The elephant needs a home," she said. She set the elephant in the box. Juliette patted it gently, like a baby.

Ms. Lewandowski, the neighbour, waved from the bench nearby. "That looks like a nice house," she said.

Rosie almost dropped the elephant. Juliette caught it with both hands. "Got you," she said softly.

The sun went down a little. Mama called, "Time to go home."

Juliette gave the box a pat. "Bye, house. Bye, car. Bye, boat."

Jimmy helped tip the box back down. They all held hands and walked to the gate.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: going to the dentist for the first time
story:
Maria sat in a big chair. It was a waiting room. Today she would see the dentist for the first time. She squeezed her mama's hand. "Will it hurt?" she asked.

A boy sat down next to her. His name was Justin. He had a loose tooth. He wiggled it with his finger. Maria watched. When he wiggled it, his whole mouth moved. She wiggled her own tooth too. Nothing happened. Her tooth stayed still. Why did his move and not hers?

The dentist called Maria in. He looked at her teeth with a little mirror. "Say hello to your front teeth," he said. "Front teeth are for biting food. Back teeth are for chewing it." Maria bit down on a soft fruit snack. Snip went the front teeth. Then she chomped with her back teeth. Chomp, chomp. The snack got small.

On the bus home, mama gave Maria an apple slice. Maria bit it with her front teeth. Then she chewed it with her back teeth. "It works!" she said. "I can feel it getting smaller." The boy across the aisle smiled at her. "Want to share mine too?" he asked. Maria took one polite little bite. Then she chewed. Chomp, chomp, chomp.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story: Henry ran out to the backyard. "Where are my toys?" he said. He wanted to build a big tower before lunch. But the toy box was empty! "Oh no," said Henry. Then he saw something funny. A string was tied to the swing. It went behind the big tree. Henry pulled the string. Out came his blocks, one by one. His dog had moved them! Henry laughed. He put the blocks in the toy box. "Blocks are toys," he said. Then he pulled again. Out came his doll. "Dolls are toys too!" He put the doll in the box. Out came his red ball. "And balls are toys!" said Henry. The box was full at last. Anais came through the gate. "Can we play?" she asked. "Yes!" said Henry. He lifted the red ball up high. "Watch me throw it far!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Aaron went to the playground with his mom. He wanted to play on the big slide. But a new boy stood by the slide. Aaron did not know him. Aaron felt a bit scared, so he hid behind his mom.

Mr. Wanjiru walked by with the new boy. Mr. Wanjiru waved at Aaron. "Hello there!" he said. Aaron peeked out from behind his mom. Would the wave still work if he hid? He stepped out a little. "Hello," said Aaron in a small voice.

Mr. Wanjiru smiled a big smile. "Hello! This is Jensen," he said. Jensen smiled too. "Do you want to send the toy elephant down the slide?" asked Jensen. He held a toy elephant. "Yes, please!" said Aaron.

Up the steps they went. Aaron slid down first. Then he sent the elephant down to Jensen. "Thank you!" said Jensen. Aaron looked at his mom. His hello had made a new friend. What else could a hello do? He waved at the swing. "Hello, swing!" he said. Jensen laughed and laughed.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: learning to play a musical instrument
story:
Jacob sat on the small blue chair. Ms. Kang handed him a recorder. It was long and white, with little round holes.

Jacob put his fingers on the holes. He blew hard. The recorder made a squeak. It sounded like a duck with hiccups. Vincent laughed. "Your duck is back," he said. Jacob laughed too. He tried again. Squeak, squeak!

"Look at your thumb," said Ms. Kang. Jacob peeked at his thumb. It was half off the back hole. He pressed it down all the way. He blew softly. A sweet, low note came out. Vincent's eyes went wide. Jacob lifted one finger. He blew again. Now the note was high, like a little bird. He lifted another finger. The bird flew even higher.

"Each hole makes a new sound!" said Jacob. He played low, then high, then low. Vincent clapped his hands. Jacob wiggled his fingers like a spider walking. The recorder sang a silly, jumpy tune. "Play it again," said Vincent. "It's my favorite song of the day." Jacob took a big breath and played the duck, the bird, and the spider, all in a row.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Rehmat ran to the bikes at the park. Her friend Lilah was already there. Rehmat jumped onto a red bike. She put her feet on the pedals. Then she stopped. She slid off the bike and ran back to the bench. "My helmet!" she said. She put it on her head. She clicked the strap under her chin. Then she got on the red bike again.

Lilah had no helmet on. "I want to ride now," Lilah said. Ms. Wardak held up a blue helmet. "Wait," said Ms. Wardak. Lilah took the helmet. She put it on too.

The two girls rode round and round the path. The sun was warm in the blue sky. A gentle wind blew on Rehmat's face. Rehmat saw her mama waving from the bench. Rehmat waved back and stayed close. Then she rang the little bell on her bike. Ding, ding! Lilah laughed. "Race you to the tree!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
story:
Nora's baby brother came home today. He was very small. He had tiny hands and tiny feet.

"Can I pat him?" Nora asked.

"Yes, but gently," said her mom.

Nora patted the baby. Pat, pat. The baby began to cry. Nora stopped. "Was that too hard?" she asked. "Yes, it was," said her mom. "A new baby must be touched very gently."

Nora looked at her hand. What could she do? She put out one finger. She stroked the baby's tiny hand. Soft, soft, soft. The baby stopped crying. The baby looked at Nora.

"Does he like soft touches?" Nora asked.

"He does," said her mom.

The window was cloudy outside. Nora saw the baby close his eyes. Soon he began to sleep. Nora whispered, "Sleep, little baby. Sleep."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
story:
Naomi woke up hungry. She wanted toast with butter. She wanted milk in her big blue cup. "I can do it myself," she said.

Her mama put two warm slices of toast on a flat plate. She gave Naomi a soft round spreader. Naomi dug the butter. The toast tried to slip away. Naomi held the plate with one hand. She spread slow and soft. The butter went all over. Every bit of the toast turned yellow.

Next came the milk. Naomi held her cup in one hand. She poured with the other. The cup wobbled. Milk made a little puddle on the table. Naomi got a cloth and wiped it up.

Then she set the cup down on the table. She let go. The cup sat still. She poured again. The milk went right in. Not one drop spilled.

Naomi took a bite of toast. She took a sip of milk. "I did it all by myself," she said. Her mama smiled. Naomi gave her cup a little pat.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Isaiah stood in the bathroom next to the big tub. Dad turned the silver tap. The water came out fast. "That side is hot," said Dad. He put his hand under the other tap. "This side is cold." Isaiah touched only the cold water. It felt like snow from the sky. Dad filled the tub with warm water. Isaiah put in his blue boat. The boat went round and round.

After his bath, Isaiah and Dad went to the store. Isaiah wanted to see the apples. He looked at the red apples. Then he looked up. Dad was not there. Isaiah looked down the aisle. He saw shoes. He saw carts. He did not see Dad.

Isaiah remembered a word Dad had taught him. The word was "worker." A worker wore a green vest. Isaiah saw a woman in a green vest at the checkout. He walked to her and held the edge of her counter. "I can't find my grown-up," he said.

The worker spoke into her phone. Soon Dad came around the corner. He knelt down and hugged Isaiah. "You did it just right," said Dad. Isaiah held Dad's hand. The apples were red and shiny in the cart.
